claim: The commonly-reported gap between verbalized confidence and token-probability confidence in LLMs is highly sensitive to unstated measurement-protocol choices, not a stable property of the model.
scope_conditions: four QA benchmarks (TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA, MMLU), three open 7-8B instruct models, no code
quoted_support: We vary the measurement axes that define the verbalized-vs-token comparison: which answer string receives the token-probability score, how that score is read from the answer tokens, and under which conditioning context it is measured.

claim: This paper is a pure measurement/methodology study; it performs no training or fine-tuning of any confidence signal.
stance_target: existence of train-time verbalized confidence work for code
quoted_support: This paper is a measurement study of confidence signals in existing open language models on public QA benchmarks. We do not train or deploy models, collect user data, or run experiments with human participants or crowdworkers.

claim: The sign and magnitude of the verbalized-vs-token confidence gap changes depending on scoring convention (Brier, NLL, AUROC, or AURC).
scope_conditions: QA domain, four scoring conventions tested
quoted_support: and may differ under Brier, NLL, AUROC, or AURC. We therefore use the [specified protocol as default].

claim: No code-generation benchmark is evaluated in this paper; scope is restricted to natural-language QA.
stance_target: code-domain coverage of verbalized confidence literature
quoted_support: We use four QA benchmarks: TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA, and MMLU.
